title: An index you can rebuild from its receipt
subtitle: Approximate-nearest-neighbour indexes are usually irreproducible, so a different result cannot be told from a bug; three hashes, a hash-seeded sample, fixed iterations and a byte-identical rebuild test make mine reproducible

stats.label: rows, the default cap on the training sample
cells at most; a configuration outside the bounds is refused
vectors at least in every cell

lede: An approximate index trades exactness for speed, and most implementations trade reproducibility away with it: random seeds from the clock, training samples that depend on traversal order, floating-point reductions whose result depends on which thread finished first. When such an index returns different neighbours after a rebuild, nobody can say whether the data changed, the build changed, or something broke. Every build produces three hashes. The configuration hash is over a canonical binary encoding of the parameters, so two builds with the same settings have the same hash regardless of how the settings were written.
quote: I wanted an index whose receipt is enough to rebuild it byte for byte.
evidence: Vector search and ANN indexes: an approximate index rebuilt byte for byte from a receipt of three hashes over its configuration, its training set and its artifact body.
Deterministic GPU computation: k-means++ seeding split so the GPU computes distances and the host draws seeds, then 25 fixed Lloyd iterations in single precision with a fixed reduction order.
Reproducible sampling: a reservoir sample seeded by a hash of the build seed and the sorted shard set, capped at 100K rows, so the same data in any order yields the same sample.
Regression testing for ML indexes: builds repeated and shuffled with one artifact hash asserted, plus a recall floor of 85% at ten neighbours against exact search.
author: Corey James
